title: Serum Institute's Cervavac Gets WHO Prequalification, Opening Path to UN Vaccine Supply
excerpt: The Pune-made, gender-neutral HPV vaccine's WHO prequalification is Serum Institute's 32nd and makes CERVAVAC eligible for procurement by UN agencies for immunization programs worldwide.
body:
• CERVAVAC®, the Serum Institute of India’s indigenously developed gender-neutral quadrivalent HPV vaccine, received prequalification from the World Health Organization, the company announced on October 5.
  • The milestone marks the 32nd WHO prequalification for Serum Institute’s products and biologicals, and inclusion on the WHO List of Prequalified Vaccines makes CERVAVAC eligible for procurement by United Nations agencies.
  • The recombinant quadrivalent vaccine targets HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18 and is indicated for girls and boys aged 9 through 26 years.
  • What this means for readers: an India-made HPV vaccine could soon flow through global immunization programs at the affordable prices Serum is known for — and it strengthens the case for expanding HPV vaccination for both daughters and sons in India itself.

From Pune to the world’s immunization programs

CERVAVAC®, India’s first indigenously developed gender-neutral quadrivalent human papillomavirus (qHPV) vaccine, has received prequalification from the World Health Organization, the Serum Institute of India announced in Pune on Monday. Inclusion on the WHO List of Prequalified Vaccines means the vaccine can now be procured by United Nations agencies and supplied to eligible countries around the world.

https://x.com/SerumInstIndia/status/2107019056369057902

"WHO prequalification of CERVAVAC® is an important step in strengthening the global response to HPV," said Adar Poonawalla, Chief Executive Officer of the Serum Institute of India. "This milestone reflects the effectiveness of the vaccine and creates the opportunity for countries to prevent HPV-related risks."

What the vaccine covers

CERVAVAC is a recombinant quadrivalent HPV vaccine that targets HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18. In girls and women aged 9 through 26, it is indicated for the prevention of cervical, vulvar, vaginal and anal cancers caused by types 16 and 18, as well as genital warts caused by types 6 and 11. In boys and men aged 9 through 26, it is indicated for the prevention of anal cancer caused by types 16 and 18 and genital warts caused by types 6 and 11.

The vaccine was previously approved for use in India by the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI). Individuals aged 9 to 14 receive it on a two-dose schedule (0.5 mL at 0 and 6 months), while those aged 15 to 26 receive a three-dose schedule (0.5 mL at 0, 2 and 6 months), administered intramuscularly. It is available in one-dose vials of 0.5 ml and two-dose vials of 1.0 ml.

An Indian-built vaccine with global partners

CERVAVAC was developed by the Serum Institute in collaboration with India’s Department of Biotechnology (DBT) and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC), along with the WHO’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) and the Gates Foundation — a public-private model that mirrors how India built its reputation as the pharmacy of the developing world.

The prequalification is the 32nd for Serum Institute products and biologicals. The Pune-based company, part of the Cyrus Poonawalla Group, is the world’s largest vaccine manufacturer, present across more than 170 countries, with an annual capacity of 4 billion doses from its Hadapsar and Manjari facilities. Its track record includes Pneumosil, the world’s most affordable pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, R21/Matrix-M, the second malaria vaccine authorized for children in malaria-endemic regions, and MenFive, the world’s first pentavalent meningococcal vaccine approved and WHO-prequalified for pediatric and adult use. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the company delivered more than 2 billion doses worldwide.

Why it matters beyond the lab

HPV vaccination remains one of the starkest global health inequities: in wealthy countries the vaccine is routine, while much of the developing world cannot afford the two or three doses needed per child. WHO prequalification is the gateway that lets UN agencies such as UNICEF and Gavi buy a vaccine for national programs, and Serum’s manufacturing scale has historically driven prices down — its stated mission since its founding in 1966.

For Indian families in India and the diaspora, the milestone also lands at home. The vaccine is gender-neutral — indicated for boys as well as girls, a point pediatricians have pressed as countries broaden HPV programs beyond cervical cancer to include anal cancers and genital warts in young men. Parents of pre-teens should know the vaccine works best before any exposure to the virus, which is why the recommended starting age is 9.

What to watch next

The real test of the prequalification is procurement: which countries and UN programs place orders, at what price, and how fast Serum’s 4-billion-dose annual capacity can scale Cervavac production. Watch for tenders from Gavi and UNICEF, and for whether India’s own universal immunization program — which currently does not include HPV — moves to add the homegrown vaccine. If both happen, Cervavac could do for HPV what Serum’s earlier vaccines did for pneumonia and meningitis: make a life-saving shot affordable wherever it is needed.
